maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in placing this motion on the Orders of the Day, my intention was to once more call the attention of the Government to a very serious domestic problem which is the cause of the unrest affecting half of our population, I am referring to the inefficiency and lack of ability of the present Board of Commerce.
Of course the matter I am referring to does not apply to the farmers who, generally speaking, are an industrious and hardworking class of people, whose prosperity and comfort are well established and which has been and is yet entitled to our admiration and best wishes. There is another class of, people who are certainly enjoying at present an unprecedented prosperity. They are known in the country as "profiteers." These men seem to have taken as a vocation that of oppressing without relaxation their fellow-men, specially the city workers whom they subject to a most vexatious system of exploitation. We are trying, by all kinds of subterfuges and tricks, to hide this social evil from those who are suffering from it, and we endeavour to convince them that the present social unrest is due merely to the reaction following every war. We know, of course, that such reaction exists everywhere, hut not to the same extent. In no other country of the world will you see what is taking place in Canada.
To-day again, I noticed in the Montreal Gazette, and I had read often before, that in the United States, instead of protecting the men who are causing such reaction, instead of giving them more power and allowing them to carry on at their own
sweet will, they arrest them, exacting in every instance a heavy hail pending their conviction which very seldom fails. In the case as reported in the Gazette this morning, it is obvious that the profiteer referred to would not have committed suicide, had he not known that he was to be convicted.
To the requests and delegations which are asking the Government to improve the condition o'f the workingmen, there seems to be always the same answer: "It is an effect of the war from which every country is suffering; work, thrift and production are the only remedies to that evil."
Mr. Speaker, they are asking our workers in the cities to pratice economy, when it is established by the Labour Gazette, that the wages they are getting are not sufficient to provide for their own families. They are asked to increase the production and then, 'the producer controls the markets; he can charge whatever prices he wishes and the workers see the product of their labour benefiting foreigners and often being used for the relief of enemies. They are asked to work. It is true that industrial and labour conferences are held and that some interest is seemingly taken in the condition of the workers by recognizing and accepting their organizations, but it is simply on the surface. In every industry the workingmen are opposed with the utmost rigour and they have great difficulty in getting the insufficient rate of wages they are getting now.
I have no hesitation in saying that the policy of the Government as far as the labour problems are concerned is completely false and misleading. Every now and then industrial conferences are called either in Ottawa, Hamilton or Montreal where there is td be one shortly and these conferences are at the pxpense of the Government. These meetings are called, the labour leaders, generally self appointed leaders-are convened as well as the leaders of industry, but there are no results. Commissions are continually being appointed, laws enacted with a view to bettering the condition of the working class and, in spite of all that, everything is at a standstill and the conditions never improve. All these commissions, if they were properly constituted, ought to have very large powers and they have none. For instance, take the commission of which Mr. O'Connor was a member. Because, one day, he acted in earnest and sincerely, he was dismissed by the Government. A certain influence had exerted itself, probably through friends

oi the Government. A little later, it was proposed to- regulate the prices of milk in Toronto. There again, some inbuence interfered and after making the regulations the commissioner was forced to alter his decision.
Then the public statement made by Hon. Justice Robson is the beist proof that these boards as constituted are absolutely of no value and completely ineffective.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if these boards are of no value and if the present methods to reduce the cost of living and to improve the condition of the working classes, are inefficient, they have to be changed. Recognizing as we do to-day the lack of ability and efficiency of these boards, we must do away with them. That is my object in submitting this resolution, in order that we may devise some more practical means to improve the conditions that obtain at present.
I think that by creating local hoards, to be composed of well informed and thoroughly independent men appointed by the local authority and who, being well known among the residents of that locality for their charity, would be able to exert a considerable influence on their fellow-citizens, justice would be better administered without any special attention being paid to any one and their descisions would be respected.
I have confidence in these local boards. I think the Government is afraid to cause their friends some trouble. In transferring their powers to these local boards their responsibility would be sufficiently sheltered so that they would not have to be uneasy on that score. Take the collection of the duties on tobacco for instance. Why is it so successful? It is because the customs officers reside in the place whose peculiarities they are perfectly conversant with. ' The same thing would occur with the local boards; they would know all the abuses committed by the profiteers and would be within the reach of those who have any complaints to lodge, whereas the present Board of Commerce travels from one city to another and the complainants can never reach them.
There is one sure thing about these local boards, Mr. Speaker-, namely, that you would certainly not see a recurrence of what has taken place in the past. We would not see any more of these profiteers, who, taking advantage of the working class, used to travel all over the county of Two Mountains, buying the whole potato crop and then leaving it there to spoil; who were doing the same thing in the county of Napierville. where the potatoes remained to rot in the

cellars of the producers; who, after shipping trainloads of these products, let them freeze on the railway sidings at Montreal; who, every spring, were filling the dumps of the city of Montreal with foodstuffs which they had hoarded and hidden during all winter to create a scarcity, and therefore an increase in the prices. We would not see any longer what occurred in the month of February of last year, when landlords increased their rents 200 per cent without any good reason and without any increase in taxes, but just because they were well aware of the fact that the housing accommodation in Montreal at the time was inadequate.
I know it is very hard for all hon. members of this House to fully realize th-e situation and the distress which obtains in our cities. Many of them enjoy the privilege of residing in the country and others,-owing to the character of their occupation, do not mingle so closely with the working people as I do. In order to know the -wants and sacrifices of the working class, you must necessarily, through your profession, follow' their ov'n way of living, to mingle with them day and night, like I do, to note what is going on in their home, be their confident as regards the abuses to which they are subjected, and the sacrifices imposed on them; be 'their attending physician, in other words, have a knowledge of their home life, arid that, every hon. member cannot have. As far as that is concerned, I am certainly more privileged than many others. Often, in the practice of my profession, I happen to meet on my way some of these people who, though their health is completely wrecked, are bound to go to work. I see often, in the morning, mothers taking their children over to the day nursery before going to eke out their means of subsistence. That is what I see as a practising physician. What is the cause of it all? It is because the head of the family has been taken away by the last war which we have gone through. As the hon. member for Ottaw'a (Mr. Fripp) stated in this House last year, the majority of the soldiers were taken out of the cities, and it is there w'here you notice the gaps, where there is want and distress, and where the disorganization occurred. Therefore, the Government ought to pay particular attention to this class of workers instead of being content with granting them sham protection such as the Board of Commerce.
Occasionally I happen to hear on my way all kinds of remarks; sometimes I have heard this expression, most unjust because it certainly is most untrue, that

the city operatives are people unwilling to work, looking after wages which are not due them. I will admit, with those critics, who are apt to indulge in rather sweeping statements, that, in our cities we have labour agitators, we have people who prejr on labour oragnizations, who make a living out of them, we have radical socialists, we have fomenters of social discords, we even have Bolsheviki in the service of petty political cliques which are not unknown to the Honourable Senator Robertson, but who surely are not representative of the spirit of the great labouring class that have for their motto one of the articles of the Liberal party's programme: Orderly progress, prosperity and welfare, of all classes.
I think it is my duty to protest as strongly as I can against such epithets as are applied to a vast majority of the labouring class. These epithets are unjust, for the workingmen, as a matter of fact, are honest, laborious and good workers, and. from the bottom of my heart I do sympathize with them when I see them struggling against a certain class of individuals whom I shall presently describe. You will remember that, in my opening remarks, I did congratulate and express my best wishes to the farming class in general, but there does exist in the vicinity of Montreal, take my word for it, a certain class of citizens who practise, in the disposing of their produce, a-system of extortion just as blamable and contemptible as the methods of those professional speculators who ply their trade in more remote quarters. From my point of view, both these classes of people have the same erroneous notion of justice and of humanity. With such local commissions as I suggest, I am sure that all these evils would disappear.
Our city workmen, Mr. Speaker, who certainly constitute one-half of the population of this Dominion, have not the advantage of breathing the pure and sunny air of our country places. From morning till night and even from night to morning, month after month, they are shut up in more or less sanitary workshops, in a foul atmosphere, breathing all sorts of dusts, of gases, both deleterious and poisonous in the spinning mills, in the white lead, sulphur, soda, quicksilver and rolling mills, in a word, all those manufactures which you recognize, as you go by, through a special sign; ambulances ever standing at the gates awaiting their victims. These people spend their days in such deleterious surroundings which greatly shorten their
lives; they are daily exposed to die and yet they labour for wages which should be doubled, trebled and quadrupled; the product of their work is sent abroad and they see their own manufactures' manager come here and testify in this very Parliament __ that, upon the product of their labour, he makes some 200 per cent profits, and, nevertheless neither the Board of Commerce nor the Government enact any legislation and take any means in order to improve their condition. I declare that is the greatest of all possible wrongs.
Everybody knows how many investigations have been held, there have been some in every country and, for its part, the present Government has quite a number to its credit. Well, Mr. Speaker, the result of all these Parliamentary inquiries shows one evident fact: It is that the cost of living will remain high as long as the producers, the wholesale dealers do not reduce the amount of their profits, as long as the profiteers, the cold storage men withhold from the people immense quantities of foodstuff which should be put on the market and that with the sole object of creating an apparent scarcity and thereby boosting prices.
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote a few statistics, reproduced by the Indianapolis News, about some big companies doing business in the United States, and in Canada as well, that have been somewhat disturbed on the American, but never on this side of the frontier. During the past few years, five companies have accumulated thousands of tons of meat, have constituted a meat trust with the sole and single object of growing richer and richer. As the following statistics may show, they have perfectly succeeded: $1,000 invested 6 years ago in the Armour Company is worth to-day $32,000; $1,000 invested in the Swift Company 6 years ago, is now worth $20,000; $1,000 invested in the Morris Company, 3 years ago, is worth at the present moment $23,000;	$1,000 invested in the Cudahy Company 6 years ago, is now worth $26,000, and $1,000 invested 2 years ago in the Wilson Company, is worth to-day $7,000.
Mr. Speaker, I have just shown the degree which human cupidity may reach when free from control, and the control of those appetites certainly requires a vigorous action, quite in contrast with that which was evidenced by the present Government up to this date. The Government will never succeed in putting them under control by

such colourless inquiries as they held when a complaint was made against a Winnipeg merchant who had thrown to the dump a great quantity of eggs, probably because they had gone bad. After the inquiry was held, the Government told us that the eggs had been thrown away for the reason that they were stale. What the country would like to know is not the reason why those eggs were thrown away, but the cause of their becomming stale to the detriment of the public. The Government will meet with no better success, either, by means of such inquiries as were held in the case of Matthews-Blackwell and William Davies, of Montreal; Rattenbury, of Charlottetown; Graham, of Belleville; Nathan Rosenstein, of Winnipeg; the Dominion Pish and Fruit, of Quebec, etc. What was the action of the Board of Commerce? In the case of the three firms first mentioned, the charge was that they had been forestalling the eggs and enhancing the price. The Board ordered them to cease selling eggs for thirty days. That was exactly what the forestallers wanted in order to determine a scarcity of this produce and to make the iprice go up. Therefore, the Government, far from dealing rigorously with them, meted out encouragement and protection in their behalf. As lor the forestallers of butter and cheese, they were forced to deliver a certain overplus to the Allies, at the market price; this was giving certain friends an opportunity to make excessive profits in their turn. I say that if all those companies find no more obstacles in their way than they did in the past, they [DOT]will act likewise in the future and continue to take advantage of the workingman while the latter will be unable to defend himself. Since the business of those companies is so widespread and so flourishing, why should they not reduce the percentage of their profits and of their dividends? If they are unwilling to do so, is not the Government, appointed as they have, been to protect the general interest of the people, in conscience bound to enact such legislation and take such steps as may be necessary to punish those unscrupulous dealers? To my mind, iwe reached the climax of indecency when, at a parliamentary inquiry, the manager of a certain manufacture stated unblushingly that the shareholders got dividends ranging from 170 to 175 per cent, and when being told that this seemed to be excessive, answered the representatives of the people that he did not work for the glory of God, but to secure the highest dividends possible for his shareholders. Did the Government take action 
against those managers, against those industries? Not at. all. Those people are evidently unaware of the principle implying that every human act should be inspired by justice and toy charity. However, we must not wonder if we happen to see those manufacturers,, profiteers and speculators at the head of benevolent associations such as the Red Cross, or at the head of protective associations, of societies for the prevention of cruelty to animals even, while in their own industries wilful murder is being committed every day.
The result of the inquiries held in every country of the world shows clearly that the high cost^ of living is due to the law of demand and supply, to impudent speculations, and, moreover, to cynical frauds and unscrupulous tactics on the part of the bulls-if I may use that expression-who are everywhere and who keep operating simultaneously in the places of production and in the great urban centres, sheltered from or tolerated by the powers that be, who refrain from using the repressive weapons put in their hands by the law; the high cost of living is due to that mad craving for wealth, to that love of money which seems to invade all the different classes of society; it is due especially to those middlemen, sheltered from all control and from all sanction, who seem to act as though they were the masters of the earth, while the Government refrains from taking any action. Why, one would almost think that the Government rather appreciates their mode of procedure.
I say that the cast of living will not be reduced as long as the Government allows those profiteers and speculators to squeeze the community and their fellowmen, instead of sending them to jail, as we see it done in the United States and in all European countries; as long as the Government fails to watch, and closely so, market fluctuations, and fails to adjust the prices in a reasonable 1 manner, so as not to check production but to eliminate that category of citizens called the middlemen, in order to save from the claws of those speculators the workingmen, who can resort only to the Government for protection. It seems that we are told not to molest those profiteers because it would be dangerous to do so, as they might strike and cause a greater evil.
I wonder since when it should be held up as a principle that evil is to be tolerated by the great mass of the people. Is it no longer dangerous to set at defiance within their last stronghold seventy-five per cent of

a population, the working class, for instance, instead of subduing those beasts of prey who live on the substance of the community. I think it an impervious duty for the Government to put a stop now, if it be not too late, to that cheating, that parliamentary clap-trap, to lay aside all the so-called progressive doctrines which can only serve the interests of a few and tickle the autocratic sentiments of a set of ninnies proficient only in trickery to an extreme degree, and to take it into their head that any policy whose immediate and direct aim is not the education of the people and the betterment of the condition of the many is a vain and dangerous policy not suitable in any sense to a democracy. Therefore I conclude that my resolution is well grounded; I fain believe the Government are not aware of all the misdeeds of those who loudly claim to be their friends, the workmen not being prone to boast of their sacrifices and sufferings. I am confident that the Government will take into earnest, and above all, practical consideration the resolution I have entered upon the Orders of the Day of the House.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that I did not hear all the speech of my hon friend, the mover of this resolution, but, as he has spoken on the high cost of living I deem it my duty to say a few words in regard to that great problem which is the subject of so much discussion at the present time. There are many causes for the increase in the cost of living. I believe that the first time that the question was brought before the House and discussed was in 1912, and, in the discussion at that time, many reasons were brought out why legislation should be enacted to prevent a further increase in the cost of living in the future.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to speak a little louder?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
I am doing the best I can. il am not the architect of this Chamber, I am very sorry. Since 1912, the war has brought about absolutely different conditions, and the profiteering which existed before the war has increased by leaps and bounds, to such an extent that the whole civilized world have had their eyes turned on that class of people. The middlemen have increased by a hundred per cent; the large number of men who were accustomed to make large profits out of the war made up their minds that after the war was over they would endeavour to continue profiteer;
ing in some other way. Those who were furnishing foodstuffs for the war, knowing the large profit they were making, made up their minds-and perhaps from a business standpoint they were right-to make as much profit after the war as during the war. Of course, they had not the same reasons for doing so. After the war was over, they could no longer make the excuse that the high price was on account of the war; that cry is passing away. But the people are suffering just the same. As I said, the middlemen have multiplied themselves to a large extent, and they are multiplying themselves very largely to-day. One special reason is that there is too much difference between the price of production and the price at which goods are sold for consumption. II admit that there are in this country many farmers who are willing to do all they can to better conditions, but there are others who are willing to do all they can to make conditions worse.
We often hear in this House that labour is so high; that transportation costs so much. If that extra cost were added on directly to the goods and the goods were sold with	the ordinary profit,
there would be some sense in the matter; but if a man is in business and if his labour costs him say twenty per cent more, he is not going to add twenty per cent to the labour alone, he is going to add twenty per cent onto the whole thing, and that I claim is absolutely dishonest. That is why there is such an unrest in the country at the present time, and the unrest now existing is merely the commencement of far worse conditions. If we do not legislate in this House and do something radical, inside of three years many hon. members here at present will see something that they will not like. The rank and file will stand about so much; they are like an animal who will stand about so much whipping and then he becomes tired and he is going to kick. The men have stood back a long time. I hear every day that the labour men of this country do not produce half as much as they used to do and they1 are asking for higher wages all the time, and, of course, the cost of production is increased on that account. The workingmen of the country are to-day having their turn; they have had the wrong end . of the deal for many years; they have asked for legislation for many years; now the condition has changed, and those who were of a very quiet spirit before have changed their minds and have decided that they are going to use the economic means at

their disposal to force, if possible, a wage commensurate with the cost of living. Some people say that it is the increase in wages that has increased the cost of living. The history of the world has not changed materially, although no doubt it has changed somewhat within the last couple of years; and history shows that increase in wages follows, and does not precede, increase in the cost of living. When people have to pay, as they do in these days, 55 to 60 cents for a dozen of eggs and about the same for a pound of butter, with other prices in proportion, how is it possible for them to live, especially in the cities. The fact is, they are not living; they are existing, and trouble is brewing. Whether the Government wants it Or not, something is going to happen and something is going to be done. We must look at conditions as they are and the men can stand just so much and no more.
If I understood my hon. friend aright, he spoke about the Board of Commerce that was appointed and that travelled throughout the country to find out how much foodstuffs were in cold storage and such like. Formerly, whenever we brought up the question of cold storage in this House, we were always confronted by the Minister of Labour with an Order in Council. He would say: The power is left to the cities; why do you not go to the cold storage companies and force them to give you the real quantity of goods they have in cold stor-aage? The Order in Council will allow you to go into the first room in the cold storage where they keep a certain quantity of foodstuffs for home consumption, but you are not allowed by the law to go beyond that door.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
How would the hon.
gentleman lower the price of wheat?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
I would be better able to tell my hon. friend if I were a farmer. I am coming back to the farmers again; I am not through with them yet. When it is said that there is a shortage of foodstuffs, that statement*is absolutely incorrect. The cold storage people say:	We are keeping
a certain quantity of foodstuffs for export. I agree that exportation must be made, but if exportation must be made, at least, it should not be made at the sacrifice of the home market as is being done at the present time. The Order in Council which was passed some few years ago looked very good on the face of it. I need not repeat its provisions because we all know them by heart. Whenever the ex-MinisteT of Labour was cornered, he used to read that Order in

Council. Some cities tried to. put it in force, but they were at once met with the difficulty that they could only investigate goods that were in storage for the home market.'Without mentioning names, I know of a man who bought over $45,000 of onions last fall. Onions are now sold at $13.50 a bag wholesale, and the consumer has to pay 15 cents a pound. A year ago last spring you could buy onions at 40 cents a bag, and that price was quite high enough. Last fall, however, they were sold for $2 a bag, and surely the farmer was making a profit at that price. Now that the wholesale price is $13.50 a bag, can any reasonable man say that an excessive profit is not being taken? No city can pass by-laws and no Provincial Government can enact legislation compelling a man to sell his goods. Traders are very touchy. As soon as you start to interfere with a man's trade he says: This is my business and I am going to handle it how I like. If, then, cities and Provincial Governments have not power to force the sale of these goods we must come to this Parliament for the necessary legislation.
I shall not speak of wheat because I am not very well versed on that subject. I shall only deal with foodstuffs, which I can .see for myself on the market every day. I do not want my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) to think I dare not touch the grain growers of the West. I would deal with wheat if I knew enough about it.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: If the- hon. gentleman is a free trader, he might tell us why he insists on legislation to govern the market.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
I insist on legislation to regulate prices.
/ Mr. BURNHAM: Where is the free trade in that?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: I do not call free trade allowing a man to sell his goods at whatever price he likes, regardless of the needs of the people. If a man is selling at an .exorbitant profit he should be called to account and be made to sell his goods at only a legitimate profit. He must give other people a chance to live. As to everyday foodstuffs, I believe there are combines handling these products. You can go through the market of any large city, Montreal, for instance, on a Tuesday or Friday morning and you will see the same price charged at both ends of the market.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Do I understand the honourable member to say that

the men who sell foi a lew dollars worth of foodstuffs on the market should be considered as farmers? These people buy from the farmers and sell their products on the markets; they are profiteers.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does
not like me to call these people farmers. He says that the people who sell these products on the market are- the market gardeners, for instance, living near a city.
I know the people I am speaking of. If there are honest profiteers, sc much the better; I take off my hat to them. I say that among the producers around a large [DOT]city there are combines. It rvas proved that in Montreal last Fall there was a combine in potatoes, but neither the city nor the Provincial Government could do anything to prevent it. I admit that there are a great many reasonable men among the farmers, but these producers around the cities are taking advantage of the very large markets they have close at hand. Furthermore, there is no middleman -between them and the consumer in the city, while in other places there may be three [DOT]or four or half a dozen middlemen between the producer and the consumer. It is obvious that a farmer -whose goods pass through the hands of three or four middlemen and eventually reach the consumer at about the same price as the products bought from the producers direct, must be selling his goods much cheaper in the first place. I know that some people are very touchy in respect of any criticism of the farmers, but 1 say that we can give the facts, for the farmers are well able to take care of themselves.
The farmer, however, has nothing to do with the cold storage plants. I should like to see the cities of this country and the Provincial Governments given power to prevent the hoarding of food in cold storage [DOT]warehouses. If they had this power the people of Montreal would not have to pay 15 cents a pound for onions, or $5 a bag for potatoes at this time of the year. I do not know whether the board that the Government appointed has made a report on middlemen and profiteers. I do not want to ,go over the ground we traversed last year and the year before. The members of this [DOT]House, regardless of the amount of money they may possess and the large amount they receive here as members, are in a position to know how much it costs to live to-day and they must know how hard it is for the common people of this country to make ends meet. Many industries in this country are making a lot of money. Take the *shoe industry, for instance. Just about three months ago you could buy a pair of very good shoes, something that is very often wanted in a big family, for $10 a pair. That was a high price. But since last January the shoe store men have [DOT]been instructed by the manufacturers to sell these same shoes for $15 a pair. They did not cost a cent more, because they were on the shelf. Because Mr. Manufacturer tells you that you cannot get any more unless you pay $5 more a pair, up goes the price to the extent of $5 or over. It may be cotton. A notice is sent out: From now on we will not furnish you with cotton unless you pay so much a yard more. The storekeeper may have a lot of cotton in stock. Up goes the price again. Is that reasonable; is that fair? If a man would say: "I am going to sell at a reasonable profit according to the price that I pay for the goods," it would be different; but when he takes advantage of the increase that they make in the factory price to put his own price up and make a profit of three hundred or four hundred per cent, I say it is wrong. .Nay I go further; I do not believe it is honest; if I will not be out of order I will say it is highway robbery. It is nothing but that. If there was a small increase it would not be so bad; there is no reason in the world why there should be such an enormous increase in the cost of the necessities of life.
They say: 'Transportation is going up and that is why we have to sell goods for so much. Perhaps it is true that to some extent transportation has gone up, but that does not account for the enormous increases that have taken place. Then they always come back and make the claim that they have been obliged to put up prices because the cost of labour is high. Take a parcel of goods worth $500 and you will find that the increase in the cost of labour that has been put upon those goods is perhaps not $10. It would be a reasonable thing for the dealer to sell those goods at $5.10. But no, he wants to secure a big price from the people and he places upon these- goods a figure that will net him three hundred or four hundred per cent.
Do you suppose that is going to last? It is impossible. Whether we want it or not, some of these fine mornings-and I would not blame them-you will see in the large cities groups of hungry men starting to go around these big stores and helping themselves. No civil power will stop them from doing so because their families are hungry.

Is it better to wait for that or to legislate, if possible, now?
I am asked what kind of legislation should be brought about. I will leave that to the Government. They can do it. I know they can. If they are not afraid of those big profiteers-and I think they are not-they will bring in legislation during the present session to regulate prices in such a way as to give a man a reasonable profit on his goods. iLet him only charge so much and if his profit is a fair one the consumer will be satisfied.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman treat profiteering in the same way as usury?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Oh, I would hang thean. I think profiteering is worse. Usury only affects a few people while .profiteering affects the whole community; jit is altogether different. There may be some people in cities who will go to borrow money at high interest but there are only a few here and there. The high cost of living and profiteering strike at the very foundations of society; they affect the people themselves. Rich and poor are affected. You speak of the high cost of living while the working people are speaking of the cost of high living. Every one is accustomed to live at a certain standard, his living formerly cost him so much but he now says that it costs him so much more. There are many people who are receiving salaries of $1,000, some less and some a little more. Will any hon. gentleman sitting at his desk take his pencil and figure out how these people live? In 1912 we were told that in this country it cost a family of five $780 to live and there were a lot of things omitted. When that was brought up in the House at that time I was asked how it was possible for a family to live on that amount. If they could not live then how can they live now? Have wages doubled? Those who are receiving $1,000 now were receiving about $700 at that time; so that there has been an increase of $300.
When you reach a certain pitch in salaries the increase stops. Smaller salaries have increased more than others. When you begin to speak of salaries people will say: That man is making 60 cents or 75 cents an hour; he ought to be satisfied. But they always forget there are 365 days in the year and that there are three meals in each day. No man will work for 365 days in the year, and not many for 300 days. Three hundred days is the maximum working time for any human being in the

course of a year. Nobody does it because in many trades climatic conditions prevent it. You rwould be surprised, at the end of the year, to see the amount of money that men receiving 75 cents an hour have made. It has been said in this House that- the .working people are spending too much money, but we seem to forget the amount they receive and we should ask ourselves .where they get the money to spend. My last word is to ask the Government whether it would be possible during the present session to enact legislation to regulate prices and put all these big profiteers in jail.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to intervene in this debate, but I wish to make a few remarks since this subject is particularly interesting to one who represents a city constituency, because he at least is enabled to express his views' on the high cost of living and on the profiteers without having his political life endangered by our friends - of the cross benches. Of course it must be well understood that the farmers from the hack lots and the back roads are necessarily not able to profit, since they have no market; I wish that to be well understood. Incidentally I am sorry that we have not heard from hon. gentlemen opposite with reference to this subject, but I should advise them that we are face to face with a situation which in a few years-probably after the next election-will be a very serious one to a large class of the community and that class will be ground between the upper and the lower millstone. We will have the horny handed sons of the soil, we will have the soldiers, we will have the labourers; a situation, so to speak-without wishing to offend any of these classes-which will bear a striking resemblance to the soldiers, peasants and workmen's delegates of Russia. The Bourgeoisie, or the Intelligentia, will then be in a somewhat difficult position. It seems to me we ought to act honestly and frankly and see that whoever is responsible for this increase in the cost of living is punished, whether by so doing we lose the soldier vote, the labour vote, or the farmer vote. Whether we represent city or town constituencies we should do the best we possibly can to place our finger on the spot from which this evil originates.
Now the farmer, as I have said, is not to my mind entirely guilty. We must take into consideration too, that he, in a large number of cases, has been imposed upon and has been placed in such a position

that he is blamed for a great deal for which he is really not guilty, by what we have called the "middleman." I know it is becoming the fashion to rail against the "middleman" because nobody seems to know who he is and therefore he is a pretty good man to hit. I have never heard any particular class of the community confess to being "middlemen."

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
What about the
lawyers?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
At the same time I think it really is possible to point to some "middlemen," and among others I would designate the cold storage people. Without going into details, and tiring the House by quoting exhaustive examples of profiteering, I have under my hand a lengthy correspondence exchanged between a very prominent citizen of Quebec and the Hon. Mr. Robertson during the year 1919. A certain example is given by this Quebec citizen which would no doubt be of some interest. In a letter dated May 25, 1919, he says:
On Thursday last a schooner from the country parts arrived in port loaded with hay. The father of one of our reporters-
This citizen is a newspaper man.-
-purchased a ton at $30 the price at which the farmers were quite satisfied to sell and make a good profit. An hour or so afterwards the entire cargo was purchased hy one of our wholesale houses and retailed at $38 to $40 per ton.
Last week a barge arrived in port from the county of Portneuf loaded with hay which the owners were ready to sell at $26 per ton. It was bought up by a local firm and immediatSly retailed at $35 per ton.
A local firm in the city on Friday last jumped the price of oats from $1.75 a hag to $1.95 giving the labour troubles of Winnipeg as a reason for the increase.
A large number of these examples have been brought to the attention of the Government and apparently not acted upon. So together with the middleman there is an accomplice, and an accessory before and after the fact, and this accomplice and this accessory is the Government of Canada.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: What action would my hon. friend suggest?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
I would repeat the suggestion of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MoMaster): Follow our advice and put in a good government. However, owing to the fact that some of my hon. friend's opposite -though a large number of them agree with me that the Government is not a very good one-wish to remain in their seats
for another couple of years, so we will find it impossible to turn the Government out at present.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
I might amend my
iquestion and ask, what immediate action would the hon. gentleman suggest?

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Let the Government resign.
, Mr. POWER:	That to my mind would
he the very best and quickest method. If I were to suggest another method to the present Government, they are so fond of delay that it would take months and months before the method would be brought into effect. However, I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) that the existing laws, together with such new laws as may be necessary, be enforced so that anybody guilty of profiteering, guilty of any offence such as I have just cited, be prosecuted, and if convicted, sentenced to a very severe penalty. This has been done in England and in France, I think it has also been done in the United States-in fact I read in to-day's Montreal Gazette that a prominent haberdasher of New York committed suicide because he was about to be convicted of profiteering in clothing. It is therefore open to the Government to take proper measures to decrease the high cost of living and bring it within reasonable bounds. But the policy of the Government on this question appears to be not to help those who may not favour them politically and not to interfere with those who favour them politically. For example, in bringing before the Board of Commerce subjects which should interest that body, they picked on an industry such as the newsprint industry which they considered one engaged in providing the necessaries of life. Newspapers are valuable, we all read them, but I hardly think-and my contention has been upheld by the Supreme Court-that they could ever have been considered necessaries of life. Even the ministers will hardly contend they were serious when they instituted proceedings against the pulp and paper manufacturers of Canada on the ground that paper was a necessity of life. If I know the'history of this agitation with reference to newsprint the policy for the control of newsprint was brought down and enforced by the Government as a fulfilment of the campaign pledges made by them in 1917. If my information is correct the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) was interested to this extent-that a very prominent paper in Toronto which is supposed to be one of his best journal-



istic supporters, had for a considerable period of , time asked that some control be placed on newsprint. And the hon. the President of the Privy-Council-a man of his word and, X have no doubt, always anxious to do the best he can to help his friends in every possible way-was only too eager, when he obtained a position in the Government, to fulfil his pledges, or at any rate to render himself more popular with the newspaper in question. Shortly afterwards the investigation was made by a Mr. Pringle, who having found that there might be profiteering in newsprint, suspected there might also be profiteering in newspapers, and wished to investigate the newspaper situation. But if my information is correct, he was told that his commission only covered an investigation of the newsprint situation. Shortly afterwards he resigned. The matter was then brought before the .Board of Commerce, with results which we all know.
While I am speaking of the newsprint matter I hope my friends opposite do not imagine that because the firm most interested in the investigation, Price Bros., come from Quebec I wish to favour them unduly. I may say for the information of hon. gentlemen that that firm is composed of what I might call the hereditary enemies of Liberalism. If there is a body of men in the province of Quebec more Tory than the members of that firm-
An hon. MEMBER-And more Unionist. Mr. POWER: Not now.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
It strikes me as being rather peculiar that Price Bros., who some years ago would not "truck nor trade with the Yankees," will now tiuck or trade with nobody else. It is not, therefore, for their sakes that I am bringing this matter before the House, but simply and solely because the newsprint industry is of great importance to the province of Quebec, giving employment to thousands of workmen, and had the action of the Government been upheld by the courts those men would very likely have been thrown out of work. It is, therefore, because I sympathize with these labourers and their families that I now refer to it. So much was this danger apparent, that newspapers like the [Montreal Gazette and the Quebec Chronicle-staunch Tory sheets-have invariably attacked the Government in reference thereto. It may be that outside of the Montreal Gazette, the other newspapers were not such large con-
sumers of newsprint that the increased price affected them to such an extent to force them to continue their support of the Government. I hold in my hand an article from L'Evenement, which my hon. friends must know is a really honest, straightforward Tory paper that has supported the Union party up till very recently. If the House will permit me I will give a rough translation. The article is in effect as follows:
Th Federal Government is not happy. It commits all kinds of blunders, but so far it has been possible for it to survive the reason for its existence. It is now about to commit a crime against those who were the first to uphold it.
Iln speaking of the control of newspapers the article proceeds:
The Government has never in any way restricted the exportation of foodstuffs, although not a day passed during the last five years when the public did not complain of the increased cost of food. To the criticisms of the people the Government answered, with considerable force, that there was this advantage for Canada, namely, that by profiting from the high prices on foodstuffs sold in the foreign markets the Canadian producer was able to maintain the commercial balance. But if that argument was a worthy one at that time, it is all the more worthy now when the exchange situation is so unfavourable to us. It seems to us that the Government is afraid of the newspapers and has favoured them in an absolutely unjust fashion to such an extent that a number of those journals most closely interested declare publicly that such administrative action is absolutely regrettable.
When I read such newspapers as L'Evene-ment, the Gazette and the Chronicle protesting that they find it impossible to further support the Government to the defence of which they have hitherto devoted their best energies, I am forced to conclude that it certainly was not the duty of the Administration to bring such a matter as the newsprint situation before our courts while, as was well said by my hon. friend from St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers), the workingmen in our cities and towns were in almost a starving condition owing to the high cost of foodstuffs.
As I said before, I had not intended to keep the House any length of time, and I apologize for having spoken so long, but I thought it was only just and reasonable that while we were on the question of the high cost of living we should examine into the manner in which the Government had abused its power with reference to matters that undoubtedly did not call for its attention.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just

taken his seat (Mr. Power) and the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Verville) in their remarks usually assure us, when there is trouble about the price of foodstuffs, that they are speaking on behalf of the poor labouring man, and they plead that some effort shall be made to arrest the rising price of commodities. I have every sympathy for the workingman and the difficulties under which he labours at the present time, but I want to say to my hon. friends that in my opinion the fault for the present condition of affairs rests much more with labour than it does with the farming community.
How incongruous it must he to our farmers to hear the labouring classes say to them: "You must produce the food we require in order to lower the cost of living," when they know that while they are working their twelve, fourteen and sixteen hours a day on the farm the labouring classes are trying to still further reduce their already shorter hours of labour. The rising costs are due not so much to the fact that wages are high as to the fact that labour in many instances will not deliver the goods. Labour is not producing to-day as it did in the pre-war days. Labour will have to take a different attitude. Labour ought to co-operate with the farmer; ought to view the work of the farmer from the proper standpoint.
Now, Sir, my hon. friend thinks that the establishment of cold storages militates against the chances of labour getting foodstuffs at lower prices. Why, only in recent years from all parts of the country requests came to the House that the establishment of cold storage facilities be encouraged in every possible way. Bounties were offered; bonuses were given; every encouragement was offered by the smaller towns to those who wished to establish cold storage plants within their precincts, so that in seasons when the supply was greater than the demand the surplus foodstuffs might not be lost. I do not think that in the conserving of perishable foodstuffs in cold storage may be found the source of the difficulties that confront us.	_
I should like to direct the attention oi the House to some significant remarks from the pen of Sir Edmund Walker. Speaking on the subject of exchange he says:
The correction of the situation cannot be permanently adjusted by the shipment of gold or sale of securities. The rehabilitation of our dollar can only be accomplished by saving, economy and greater production. The rising curve of prices cannot be made to turn downward without an increase of production, nor
74i
can we face the heavy obligations left by the war except by greatly increasing production. The man who does not do his best at his particular job is not merely helping to barricade the only pathway that will lead us out of our troubles, but he is helping to raise, or to maintain, the cost of the necessities of life for his own family. I may be called a friend of capital for saying this, but I am on record elsewhere as an advocate of many changes in the present relations of the employee and employer, all of them in favour of the employee.
While we and the rest of the world are failing to produce on a sufficient scale to provide for human comforts, and to pay our debts, the price of everything has so increased, that although all clearing-house and trade returns show higher figures in money, these generally represent transactions based on smaller quantities of merchandise, and because we think in terms of dollars and not of merchandise, we are living in a fool's paradise.
Then he goes on to say, with regard to purchasing at home:
For every purchase of goods made abroad, whether in Great Britain or China, or anywhere else, we settle through New York, and the rise or fall of the rate of exchange, about which we are so much concerned, is the expression of our failure, or the reverse, to pay cash or its equivalent.
The member for St. Denis argues that the largely increased price of potatoes at the present time over the price last Fall -I think he quoted the present price at $5 a bag-is evidence of profiteering on the part of the farmer. Well, if he thinks that the fixation of prices of agricultural products will bring about lower prices, he is making a great mistake. It is the unsettled and uncertain condition of the country and the constant whining about the prices of the products of the farmer that is causing the slackening of production. So long as the export markets available to this country give a fair price for the products of the farm, that price will be the price commanded by the farmer for similar products sold in Canada. The present price of potatoes is not the result of potatoes being held in cold storage or their being carried over from last year. If Canada had now in the dump basket her total production of potatoes of last year she would not begin to have enough to supply the demands of our friends across the line, a large portion of whose crop was destroyed. Potatoes are $5 a bag to-day because the buyer in the United States needs our product and is willing to pay the price. Then why talk nonsense about the farmer profiteering and about the prices of farm products advancing? Let us get away from that attitude; let us get in sympathy with the man on the farm, in order that we may encourage him to greater production. We are asking

the farmer, and justly so, to bend every effort toward largely increased production. If you want larger production from the land, the best way to encourage it is to give the farmer the assurance of stability of prices.; you will not encourage him by bickering with him, whining about his prices, and trying to create the impression that he is a profiteer. If he grows and produces it is not a matter of cost; it is a matter of what the world's markets will give him for his products; that is what he is honestly entitled to obtain. It does hot come well from labour or from those in the city who work in offices or follow professional callings, and who work perhaps only seven hours a day, to criticize the man who labours from twelve to sixteen hours a day.

maintopic: THE BOARD OF COMMERCE-MOTION FOR ITS ABOLITION AND THE CREATION OF LOCAL BOARDS TO REPLACE IT.
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman pretend that the professional man, the lawyer or the doctor, works only seven hours a day?
, Mr. GLASS: Well, to answer my hon. friend honestly, I would not think he works that much. My hon. friend argued that it was not the farmers far distant from the cities who were the profiteers-and that is not a very pleasant word, I submit, to throw at them-it was the truck farmer, the man living close to the city, who was getting the high prices. I live in the centre of a country which carries on a large truckfarming business. There the truck gardeners gather from all around and sell their commodities in the open market at the prices which the public are willing to givA The reason why prices are higher in the city is not that the farmer is trying to force a higher price; it is the inevitable working of the law of supply and demand. There is a greater demand for the commodities in the city, and the price is that which the consumer is willing to pay:	Early vegetables come from the United States in the early part of the year, and the prices in our country closely follow those of the products that come in from the other side. I sub-'mit that the law of supply and demand regulates the prices in the markets close to the cities. That, to my mind, is evidence of the importance to the farmer of the home market, which at the present time consumes over eighty per cent of the entire products of Canadian farms.
There are some further remarks of 'Sir Edmund Walker's which I should like to quote, but Sir Edmund Walker's opinion expressed in w'hat I have read is, I think, really the crux of the whole matter. If we are going to improve conditions and

lower the cost of living, it must be by getting efficiency in our labour and by working longer hours. In this great reconstruction crisis of this country and of the world, if labour had fully met national needs, labour would have given longer service and the most efficient service possible to increase the production of commodities, because it is only in that way that we can hope to have lower price levels. Sir Edmund Walker makes some observations with reference to the process of adjustment, and I take the liberty of quoting him because what he says is very cogent and forceful and 'bears on the case. He says:
The difficulties of reconstruction after the great war are even greater than we feared. The whole world is feeling the effect of four years in which the ordinary work and economics of life were not merely neglected, but the basis thereof was almost swept away. We are short of almost every commodity, the strongest evidence of this being the fact that millions of people in Europe face actual starvation. We cannot re-establish the normal supply of commodities except toy working harder than usual, and we cannot lessen the terrible strain of high prices without doing the extra work which will put an end to the lack of commodities. We cannot adjust prices without also bringing about a contraction in the volume of paper money and other instruments of credit, and so far as it is possible to enforce contraction without interfering with the production of what is really necessary, the reduction of prices will be facilitated. In a word, bankers should not aid speculation, or assist ventures which do not directly lead to production. We are still building ships with feverish haste throughout the world, and we ought to be spending large sums on railroads in order that commodities may be freely distributed. The present cost of ocean transportation, quite as much as the cost of goods at the primary market stands like a huge barrier across the pathway of return to normal conditions. x What is worse, however, is that even present prices, in the natural order of things, will go on rising until the lack in the world's supply of commodities has been filled, and there has been a large contraction in the volume of paper money now in existence	 Prices will be higher than before
the war for many years to come, but a readjustment to tolerable conditions is absolutely necessary if we are to enjoy the peace bought at such a cost. Governments must cease borrowing and keep their expenditures within their powers of taxation; both individuals and governments must spend less on things not absolutely necessary, and we must all work harder to produce the normal supply of all the commodities useful in life.
Speaking of co-operation, Sir Edmund Walker says in a few words:
Canada won its high place in the world's regard by superb co-operation in the one idea of winning the war. Can we not compromise for the moment the differences between capital and labour, between farmer and manufacturer, between the various interests that are risking our future for the sake of their own particular grievances, and co-operate. in another idea.

equally great, the restoration of peace and the return of prosperity on a better foundation? With this accomplished the separate ideals of the industrial divisions of our society can be discussed with far more chance of fair adjustment than is possible in these difficult times.
Just in conclusion, I say to my hon. friends who find so much at fault with conditions on the farm and the increased cost of living, that if labour and all other interests would co-operate in lending encouragement to increased production on the farm, we would much sooner see the end of the difficult situation which confronts us. Not only is a kinder sympathy and sentiment towards the producer of the soil necessary, but an earnest, sincere desire on the part of labour itself to do its share in this reconstruction, is essential. If wages are higher and hours are eight hours a day, then labour must do eight hours' efficient work; it must deliver the goods. That is what is essential on the part of labour, if it is to do its share in this period of reconstruction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this -debate, but I feel constrained to do so following the brief remarks of my hon. friend, the member for St. Denis (Mr. Verville), who, a few moments ago, described to us the ordinary farmer, as a man coming three times a week to sell his products on the city market. That man, Mr. Speaker, is not a farmer at all; he is .simply a middleman; more than that, he is a profiteer. As a rule, such a man -does not own a farm. He travels through the country, buying from the farmers products which he isells the following day at exhorbi-tant prices on the city market, he is in short that individual whom the hon. member for St. Denis described a few moments ago as deserving to be hanged.
In the minds of some city people the farmer should meekly allow himself to be cheated out of his due, letting all the profits go to the middleman. Some speakers complained of the high price of all commodities. They think that they are being fleeced when called upon to pay 80 cents for a pound of butter and $5 for a bag of potatoes. It is exceedingly high, they say; it is outrageous and revolting for the workingman to pay such prices. However, it would be well to make the public realize that this butter for which the working man to-day pays 80 cents a pound is really the same commodity which the farmer sold 45 cents a pound last fall, while the potatoes which are retailed this very day at $5 a bag, in Ottawa, were bought from the farmer at the rate of 90 cents or $1.10 a bag. You must admit with me, Mr. Speaker, that the profits allowed to the farmeT are very small compared with those which the middleman gets as intermediary between the producer and the -consumer,
In my opinion one of the best means of reducing the high cost of living, would be first to speak o>f it less frequently and to do more work. Some hon. members-and I don't blame them for that-who represent certain manufacturing centres in this Parliament, when the eight hour day is being discussed, are the first to say; "We are in favour of an eight hour day for the workingman." In my opinion, one of the factors of the increase in the cost of living is the eight hour day. I believe that the best suggestion which I could offer would be to at once start a campaign for the purpose of satisfying the- workingman that he is not being despoiled by the farmer and that it is not fair for him, as a consumer, to ask. for an eight hour day's work, while he requires that the farmer should stay at work during fourteen or fifteen hours a day for the production of the foodstuffs he requires. These are so many reasons, or * conditions, which make for the increase of the cost of living.
Mr. d'ANJOU (Rimouski) translation): Mr. Stpeak-er, I would not like to allow this resolution to be adopted without adding a few words.
I listened with great attention to the speeches which have been delivered, especially by some of my hon. friends who represent divisions in the city of Montreal. They seem to hold the farmer responsible for the soaring of the prices of commodities. I cannot agree with them at all on that point. As the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Fafar-d) stated a -few moments ago, the farmer is not to blame; we must lay the blame at the door of the middleman, who buys the products from the farmer with a view to hoarding them in cold storage in warehouses, where they deteriorate, instead of -placing them upon the market. Consequently it is absolutely unfair to charge the-farmers with profiteering. Moreover, we must take into consideration the fact that if they sell to-day their products at higher prices than formerly, it- is -due to. the increase in the (cost of labour and of farming implements. Therefore, they are perfectly justified in increasing to a certain extent the price of their products; but I say again, the only profiteers are the middlemen.
Farmers work from sunrise to sunset; they are toiling on land, toiling hard and;

continuously, and therefore, they ought to be rewarded ifor their work.
In my opinion, the best means, the most efficacious method for checking the high cost of living, is not in bringing down resolutions to that effect in this House; nor in casting reflections or slurs upon the farming community, but in intensifying farm production, in creating an army of tillers of the soil, in starting a live campaign. The object of which would be to attract young men back to the land, en to stem the rush to cities, and in offering them every possible inducement to remain on the farm; furthermore in taking the taxes off agricultural implements and other accessories of life.
It must not be lost sight of that in this country, as everywhere else, consumption is increasing and production is on the wane. Therefore equilibrium should be restored, and production must keep pace with consumption. In order to remedy that evil, it behooves the Government to look more closely after the interests of the farming industry; it is up to them to spend considerable sums of money, if need be, so as to further that end, and as I said, to readjust the tariff and take the taxes off agricultural implements and the necessaries of life. 1 am satisfied that by such means the desired end will be reached.
There is not the slightest doubt that the Board of Commerce, created by the Government, has proved, like all those other boards, an unqualified failure; but I do not think that it is by doing away with it that you will succeed in bringing down the high cost of living. As I said, you should encourage agriculture, more liberally than you have done so far, and such encouragement will be a solvent of the important problem -which has been under consideration "to-day.

The House resumed, from April 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12, respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Mr. Guthrie. Mr. Morphy in the Chair.
On section 77-how disagreements as to taxation of expenses settled:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood this section was to be regarded as contentious.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I had it marked to stand, too.
Section stands.
On section 78-election expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This section is a compilation of the law which has been in force in this country for many years, and also of some sections taken from the English Act. As the Committee is probably aware, the provisions in the English Act in regard to the payments by candidates for personal expenses, or for the cost of an election, aTe

*much more drastic than they have ever been 'in this country. All the sections of the English Act which would be applicable to conditions in Canada have been incorporated in the present section, and the Committee will see that the restrictions are very great. The idea was not only to keep down the expense of elections on the one hand, but to see that purity in election contests is maintained on the other. For that reason the draftsman of this Bill has incorporated the stringent provisions of the English Act. Personally I see no objection to them.
Why are payments made fifty days after an election instead of thirty days?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think fifty days is
a very fair period.
Would it not be just as fair to make it thirty days? Why keep these accounts hanging around?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is not a matter of much moment.
I think the period ought to be thirty days. I do not see why we should make any change at all. Thirty days is quite long enough to keep election bills open.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know. It might be that in settled portions of the country thirty days is a long enough period, but there are other constituencies, not so well settled, where it is not easy to get around. The distances are long, and the means of communication not very ready. I think fifty days is a very reasonable period.
Does the Bill define what is meant by the "personal expenses" of a candidate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is to be found on page 2, paragraph (r).

The definition set out there is very general. It includes "the reasonable travelling expenses of such candidate and the reasonable expenses of his living at hotels or elsewhere," and "all other expenses which, except as restrained by this Act, he may in person lawfully incur and pay." If I understand the definition well, a candidate can personally pay for the printing of the voters' list. That is a legal expenditure. He can personally pay the rent of a hall in which to hold meetings. That is also a legal expenditure. He can pay many other expenses, including the cost of committee rooms. But by the section
under consideration you limit the personal expenses of a candidate to the sum of $500. Has the Government thought over the fact that after the next redistribution the constituencies will be laTge? The population of the province of Quebec, which is the basis upon which representation is made, has grown very much, and according to the latest statistics the unit of representation for each constituency, instead of being nearly 30,000, will be nearly 40,000. Therefore the candidate will have a larger constituency and his personal expenditure will certainly be greater. Consequently, I believe that the limit of $500 fixed by this section is altogether too restricted. With the proposed system of enumeration a candidate will have to incur personal expenses to survey the registration of the electors in his constituency, and those expenses will be increased to such an extent that $500 will be altogether inadequate. It must be remembered that candidates cannot always travel by train or trolley car, and they are obliged to hire automobiles at a cost of at least $25 a day in addition to the living expenses of the chauffeur. This restriction to $500 applies during the election, and that is defined in subsection (d) of section 2 in this way:
during an election" or ''at an election" or "throughout an election" includes the period after the issue of the writ for an election, or after the dissolution of Parliament or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of which a writ for an election is eventually issued, until the elected candidate is returned as elected;
According to this definition that period may extend over a couple of months. Does the Government believe that such a restriction is reasonable? For my part I shall be willing to move that the section be amended so as to allow a personal expenditure. of $1,000. It is no use to support the five-hundred-dollar limitation on the ground that you want to secure purity of elections. I am just as anxious as the Government to work to that very desirable end, but I do not want to be a hypocrite, and I assert that in my constituency a sum of $500 is totally insufficient to cover the personal expenditure of a candidate during an election which may last two months. I believe that every hon. member who has had any experience of elections will bear me out. For this reason I move:
That the words ''five hundred dollars" in line 30 on page '58 and in line 23 on page 60 he replaced by the words "one thousand dollars."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think
my hon. friend does not quite apprehend

the meaning of the section. The five-hun-dred-dollar limitation is not a limitation of personal expenses, it is the limitation of what a candidate may himself pay, his agent must pay anything over and above the $500.
I am obliged to have my agent with me all the time in that case.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: I understand the meaning of the section perfectly well.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no limitation
to $500 in the section.
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken. He may expend more, but any amount in excess of $500 has to be paid out by the agent, not by the candidate himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think so.
Then the amount should be very much more in our Act. The candidate in England is never very far away from his agent, whereas one constituency in this country may be as large as the whole of England.

My constituency is forty-eight miles by one hundred and eighty miles and there is no railroad in it. You will appreciate what it means to travel around that constituency in a motor car. Moreover, we have not garages out in that country which can afford to wait thirty or sixty days for their money. Usually the owner depends on one car for his living; he has to pay cash for gasoline, and often you have to pay him in advance in order that he may be able to provide himself with the necessary equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Why should the agent not be asked to arrange the transaction in that case?
In a large constituency your agent cannot cover the whole ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You are entitled to more than one agent.
Well, if you want to keep down election expenses, you cannot have a dozen or more agents in all parts of the constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This provision is not aimed at agents; it is designed to prevent the candidate from spending money at election time for the purpose of making

friends and getting votes. It is to eliminate as far as possible any expenditure on behalf of the candidate. He is given an allowance of $500, but if his legitimate personal expenses run to $5,000 that is all right, provided they are paid by his agent; the candidate may not himself disburse an amount in excess of $500. There is nothing here which provides that the agent shall not pay all legitimate expenses. I cannot conceive that a candidate will be occasioned any great inconvenience, because he is permitted to have an agent to make these bargains.
Do I understand the minister to say that the candidate may have several agents?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is power for the agent to appoint an agent. Of course, it has to be done in writing; the authority has to be definite. However, this clause appears to be contested, and under our agreement it will have to stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: With respect to subsection (7), which is taken from the English Act, it, may be that the time fixed there is all right as far as England is concerned, but it might work an injury in regard to some of the constituencies in this country. ting it in the day after an election if he so desires.

Subsection (5) provides for
publishing the returns in detail in a newspaper published or circulated in the electoral district. Suppose no newspaper was published in the district, and that a candidate selected a newspaper of which only five copies were circulated in that district,
