On section 80-bribery, treating, undue influence and personation:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is an
omission of a few words that are found in the old Act, and I would like to ask the minister if it has any significance. In subsection (e), page 65, line 16, the subsection reads:
Advances or pays, or causes to be paid, any money to or to the use of any other person with the intent that such money or any part thereof shall be expended in bribery at any election.
In the old Act it read "shall be expended for bribery or corrupt practices in any election." Would it not be better to keep these words in?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the Act is differently constructed. The former section was 265, and it began with the declaration that every person who directly or indirectly does so-and-so shall be disqualified for a term of eight years, and so on. The present Bill is drawn upon a different plan. It begins:
Every person is guilty of the corrupt practice of bribery and of an indictable offence-
And so on. Bribery itself is a corrupt practice and bribery is included amongst these things which are enumerated and declared to he corrupt practices. By the first line in the section bribery is declared to be a corrupt practice punishable under this Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is also a difference in subsection (f), where it speaks of the giving of a "valuable consideration for any office, place or employment." The old Act added "or for the promise of any office, place or employment." Should that be dropped?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to these words being added to the subsection.
I would therefore move that the words "or for the promise of any office, place or employment or" be added after the word "or" in the last line of subsection (f). Amendment agreed to.
Will the minister explain to the committee what period is covered by the expressions "before the election" and "after the election" mentioned in paragraphs (g) and (h)?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
"During an election,
after an election and throughout an election" are defined as including the period after the issue of the writ for an election, after the dissolution of Parliament, or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of which a writ for an election is eventually issued, until the elected candidate is returned elected.

Is that the interpretation of the law?
iMr. CANNION: What about the word "before" in paragraph-(g)?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
"Before an election"
would be that period before the issue of the writ, because, as is well known, the candidates are sometimes a long time in the field, indulging actively in canvassing, making speeches, and the like. (I presume it would apply to the time before the issue of the writ.
There is no limitation as to time at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The courts have decided that when a man announces himself as a candidate, that is the time when he really becomes the candidate.

The minister probably
knows that some people are perpetual candidates. Therefore according to the definition given by the minister it would be any time at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In that case we will have to allow good judgment and common sense to govern.
Section as amended agreed to.
-On section 81-treating of any person.
iMr. McKiBNZIE: Is this the same section as in the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is an adaption of two sections in the old Act and a few words from the English Act.
Mr. McKENZIE.: It is rather a dangerous experiment to be changing the sections at all unless for a really good purpose. We have had a great many election trials in this country and the decisions in those trials have been given under the sections in the old Act. If we now change those

sections we practically destroy the effect of all those decisions. Unless there is really some good purpose to be served we should refrain as much as possible from making any changes.
'Mr. GUTHRIE: I agree in the main with the statement of my hon. friend, but I think the present section is much more comprehensive, and at the same time much more clear, than the other two sections were together. I think the present section is a decided improvement on the old language. While the meaning and scope is preserved, I think the offences described in the section are much more clearly described and in better language. At the same time, as a general rule I think it is as well to maintain as far as possible the exact language. That has been done, I think, in the drafting of this measure.

The section reads "any person who corruptly," and so on. Why should the word "corruptly" be placed there?
Mr. (GUTHRIE: To what part of the section does my hon. friend refer?
To the third line of section 81 where it says "who corruptly." Is not the act supposed to be corrupt?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose there may be an innocent act under the language of that section. The old law has maintained the word "corruptly" and we have continued it in this Bill. You may innocently do a thing not for the purpose of influencing a vote, which is forbidden in the section. If you did it for the purpose of influencing a vote it would be corrupt. I can distinguish between an act of charity and a corrupt act, and it is to safeguard the acts of pure innocence-
The salvation of candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-that the word "corruptly" is put in. No, I do not think for the salvation of candidates. I think it is a generally accepted term, it has been in our election law for many years. The motive of a man's act must be established.
(Mr. CANNON: If it becomes a question of intent how could any judge or any court penetrate the intentions of a party or person?	_

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: By overt acts.

Suppose I were brought before the courts under section 81 I would
only have to prove that I had no corrupt intention, If there is no "mens rea" there is no crime. I think if the clause is to mean anything the word "corruptly" should be struck out, otherwise there can be no conviction if the accused has a lawyer who knows anything about criminal law and the criminal intent which has to be connected with the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A great many cases have been prosecuted under that section. The burden of proving the corrupt intention has been on those who set it up, and they have succeeded. The corrupt intention must be presumed from acts and language as well as from mental attitude. It is a word so well known in the jurisprudence of this country that I would hesitate to strike it out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The word "corruptly" is used twice. The section says that every person who "corruptly" does what is mentioned for the purpose of "corruptly" influencing. I should think that one "corruptly" would be sufficient. The section should apply to any person who corruptly does the thing described for the purpose of influencing, or does it for the purpose of corruptly influencing.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it hurts the section at all, although it might be just as well to have but the one. I would not like to change it though.

For the good of the candidate's friends in a free country like the province of Quebec 'I would suggest that we strike out the word "corruptly" because otherwise all the time during which a man is a candidate he will not be able to treat his friends at all; they will have to go round with him and look after him and to see that hospitality is dispensed with. I think it is rather absurd.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How did they get on in the past in that' respect?
In the past there was only a period of eight days. The candidate was therefore only a burden to his friends for that short time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, he was a candidate from the date of the issue of the wrjt? The law in that respect has not been .changed and the word "corruptly" was always in the statute. ,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would think that if the word "oorruiptly" were omitted before the word "influencing" it would make the intention of the section clearer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That language is identical with the language in the old Act. The old law applied to every candidate "who corruptly by himself and others for the purpose of corruptly influencing." I think if I were' drafting that section I would have put in one "corruptly" but 1 would not like to change it now. I do not think it hurts any.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 82-undue influence; false pretence interpreted.
Mr. M'cKENZIE: Is this section different from the old section?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The framework is altered, the other section starting out differently, but the sense is the same.
Mr. PARENT; Would my hon. friend give us the definition of "spiritual injury"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think perhaps Sir
Oliver Lodge might be qualified to do so, but I am not.
Is that a new addition?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Those words "temporal or spiritual" were not in the old law.

I move, Mr. Chairman,
that the words "spiritual injury" be struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
For what reason?
Mr. PARENT':	I cannot hear from my
hon. friend any reason why those words should be inserted there. I do not see how we can find out or estimate "spiritual" injury.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose the meaning
of the words is a threat of some injury in this life or in the life hereafter. I think that such a threat operating on a weak-minded individual might be serious. Therefor I can see no objection to the words remaining. I may say, however, that I do not think they are of very great efficacy. Section agreed to.
On section 83-personation and subornation of personation.
I have had no time to study the Bill, but I rather fear this section does not cover the case of a man who, having no right to vote, comes forward and asks for a ballot in his own name.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That would not be an offence unless he takes the oath. It has always been permitted to a man to ask for the right to vote, and he may, through ignorance, think he has that right. The 
test is: Will he be sworn? If he takes the oath, then he is liable under the criminal law as well as under the provisions of this Bill. This section does not prevent a man asking for a vote, unless he does it fraudulently.
Does this Bill provide for one man one vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Subsection (b) reads "having voted once at such election," and so on. Supposing a person votes in a neighbouring constituency?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
He would be guilty of
an offence under this Bill; and punishable at law. It is provided that he shall vote once in the constituency in which he resides.

Is an elector entitled to
only one vote at an election, or is he entitled to one vote 'in two or more constituencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No; the principle of
one man one vote has been adopted.
In what particular clause is that specified?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It certainly is specified in the oath.

It also means one
woman one vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
If he does not swear he can vote many times.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If he does he renders
himself liable to the penalties prescribed.
I think there is a declaration in one of the clauses that stood over that a man can vote only where he resides.

I do not think so. I remember looking through the Bill and thinking that the attention of the committee should be called to this matter. Under our provincial law we have one man one vote, but up to the present time under the federal law in Quebec a man has been able to vote in two or three constituencies if his name is on the lists.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 29 I think covers it. The qualifications of an elector under subsection (c) is that he has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ. He is not qualified unless he complies with that subsection. So he must

vote where he resides, and he can reside in only one place for two months.

Take the case of a man
who has property in one constituency in the country and is placed on the list in respect of that property; within two months of the election he moves into a city and is placed on the city list. Is there anything to prevent him voting in both constituencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

How?
Mr. PARDEE!: He does not reside in the country any more.
(Mr. GUTHRIE:	He has to take an oath
that he has resided for at least two months-in the constituency in which he is voting.
He would be challenged.

I call the attention of the
minister to section 32.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That was allowed to
stand.

It refers to this same thing. Subsection (9) speaks of a person who applies to be again registered in the same electoral district, which to my mind rather implies that he could ask to be- enrolled in another electoral district.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Because the Act deals with it on the basis of residence, and I believe that residence should govern.

The dividing line between two constituencies in Ontario runs through the centre of a man's farm. On one side is his house; on the other his barns and the houses in which his hired help live. This man is in one constituency as much as in the other, for he works as much about his barns as about the house. Is he regarded as having residence in two constituencies, and if so, is he allowed to vote in two constituencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Under this Bill, as under the Ontario law, there would be no difficulty in deciding that question. The house in which he lives would be his residence.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Progress reported.
